group.passage: When Wangari Maathai learned in 2004 that she had won the Nobel Peace Prize, she did not throw a party. Instead, she went outside and planted a tree. For a woman whose life's work had begun with a handful of seedlings, it was the most natural way to celebrate. Maathai was born in 1940 to a farming family in the highlands of central Kenya. Unusually for a girl of her generation, she went on to study biology in the United States. After returning home, she earned a doctorate, something no woman in East or Central Africa had done before, and she later taught at the University of Nairobi. Yet her attention was increasingly drawn to the hardships of rural women, who lacked clean water and wood for their cooking fires. In 1977, Maathai started the Green Belt Movement, which taught women to plant trees on their farms and around schools and churches. The trees helped keep water supplies clean and provided fuel, while the women who tended them gained skills and a sustainable way to support their families. Over the years, the movement has helped plant over 40 million trees in Kenya. Her work did not win universal approval. Those in power at the time regarded her as a threat, yet she persevered, and planting trees became a peaceful way of defending ordinary people and their rights. This eventually earned her respect far beyond Kenya. In 2002, she was elected to the national parliament with 98 percent of the vote, and two years later she was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize, the first African woman ever to win it. Why would a peace prize go to someone known for planting trees? Maathai explained that many conflicts begin as struggles over limited resources such as land and water. When those resources are damaged or scarce, competition for them grows, and competition can lead to violence. Managing nature responsibly, she argued, is therefore one way of protecting peace. She died in 2011, but her legacy endures: the African Union now honors her every year on March 3, known as Wangari Maathai Day.

translation_zh.text:
種樹的諾貝爾和平獎得主

2004 年，旺加里‧馬塔伊得知自己獲得諾貝爾和平獎時，她沒有舉辦派對，而是走到戶外種了一棵樹。對一位畢生志業始於一把樹苗的女性而言，這是最自然的慶祝方式。

馬塔伊 1940 年出生於肯亞中部高地的一個農家。在她那個年代的女孩中很少見地，她後來到美國攻讀生物學。回國後，她取得了博士學位——在東非與中非，在她之前還沒有任何女性做到——之後在奈洛比大學任教。然而，她的注意力越來越被鄉村婦女的困境所吸引——她們缺乏乾淨的水，也沒有煮飯用的柴火。

1977 年，馬塔伊創立了「綠帶運動」，教婦女在自家農地和學校、教堂周圍種樹。這些樹有助於保持水源乾淨並提供燃料，而照顧樹木的婦女也學到技能，有了可長久養家的方式。多年來，這個運動已協助在肯亞種下超過 4,000 萬棵樹。

她的工作並未受到所有人的認同。當時的掌權者把她視為威脅，但她堅持不懈，種樹成了以和平方式捍衛一般人民及其權利的途徑。這最終為她贏得了肯亞以外的廣泛尊敬。2002 年，她以 98% 的得票率當選國會議員，兩年後獲頒諾貝爾和平獎，是第一位得到這個獎的非洲女性。

為什麼和平獎會頒給一位以種樹聞名的人？馬塔伊解釋，許多衝突始於對土地和水等有限資源的爭奪。當這些資源受損或變得稀少時，對它們的競爭就會加劇，而競爭可能導致暴力。因此她主張，負責任地管理自然，就是保護和平的一種方式。她於 2011 年辭世，但她的影響延續至今：非洲聯盟現在每年在 3 月 3 日紀念她，這一天被稱為「旺加里‧馬塔伊日」。
